\chapter{Chapter05 — Rademacher First Moment}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from FABL.Chapter05.RademacherFirstMoment
\section{Overview}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{FABL.Chapter05.RademacherFirstMoment}.

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Uniform Rademacher measure]
\lean{FABL.rademacherMeasure}
\statementsource{vershynin-hdp-book}{
  pdf-681b6f3d947f-p023-b003,
  pdf-681b6f3d947f-p153-b003,
  pdf-681b6f3d947f-p153-b006
}
\label{FABL.rademacherMeasure}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.uniformPMF}
For each natural number $n$, define the Rademacher measure on the $n$-dimensional
Boolean cube to be the measure induced by the uniform probability mass function on that
cube.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Rademacher summand]
\lean{FABL.rademacherSummand}
\statementsource{vershynin-hdp-book}{
  pdf-681b6f3d947f-p023-b003,
  pdf-681b6f3d947f-p153-b003,
  pdf-681b6f3d947f-p153-b006
}
\label{FABL.rademacherSummand}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.signValue}
For a natural number $n$, a real-valued coefficient function $a$ on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, an
index $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and a point $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, define the $i$th Rademacher
summand to be $a_i$ times the sign represented by the $i$th coordinate of $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Sum of Rademacher summands]
\lean{FABL.sum_rademacherSummand}
\label{FABL.sum_rademacherSummand}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.linearForm, FABL.rademacherSummand}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ be real coefficients, and let $x$
be a sign vector of length $n$. The sum of the Rademacher summands $a_i x_i$ is the
linear form $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Product form of the Rademacher measure]
\lean{FABL.rademacherMeasure_eq_pi}
\label{FABL.rademacherMeasure_eq_pi}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.rademacherMeasure, FABL.uniformPMF, FABL.uniformSample_toMeasure_eq_pi}
\difficulty{1}
For every nonnegative integer $n$, the uniform probability measure on the finite cube
$\\{-1,1\\}^n$ equals the product, over its $n$ coordinates, of the uniform probability
measure on $\\{-1,1\\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Mean of a sign coordinate]
\lean{FABL.integral_signCoordinate_eq_zero}
\label{FABL.integral_signCoordinate_eq_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.expect_monomial, FABL.integral_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.monomial, FABL.rademacherMeasure, FABL.signValue}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number and choose a coordinate $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$. For a
uniformly distributed sign vector $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, the expected value of its $i$th
coordinate is zero.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Mean of a Rademacher summand]
\lean{FABL.integral_rademacherSummand_eq_zero}
\label{FABL.integral_rademacherSummand_eq_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.integral_signCoordinate_eq_zero, FABL.rademacherMeasure, FABL.rademacherSummand}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $a=(a_i)_{i=1}^n$ be real coefficients, and let
$i\in\{1,\\ldots,n\theta$ be a coordinate. For a uniformly distributed sign vector
$x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, the expected value of $a_i x_i$ is zero.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Independence of Rademacher summands]
\lean{FABL.rademacherSummands_iIndep}
\label{FABL.rademacherSummands_iIndep}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.rademacherMeasure, FABL.rademacherMeasure_eq_pi, FABL.rademacherSummand, FABL.signValue, FABL.uniformPMF}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number and choose real coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_n$. Under the
uniform probability measure on $\{-1,1\}^n$, the random variables $x\mapsto a_i x_i$,
for $i=1,\ldots,n$, are mutually independent.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Integrability of a Rademacher summand]
\lean{FABL.rademacherSummand_memLp}
\label{FABL.rademacherSummand_memLp}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.rademacherMeasure, FABL.rademacherSummand, FABL.signValue_eq_neg_one_or_one}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb{R}$, and let
$i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$. On the uniform probability space of sign vectors $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$,
the random variable $x\mapsto a_i x_i$ belongs to $L^p$ for every exponent
$p\in[0,\infty]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Variance of a Rademacher summand]
\lean{FABL.variance_rademacherSummand}
\label{FABL.variance_rademacherSummand}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.integral_rademacherSummand_eq_zero, FABL.integral_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.rademacherMeasure, FABL.rademacherSummand, FABL.signValue_eq_neg_one_or_one}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $a:\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\to\mathbb R$, and choose a
coordinate $i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. On the uniformly distributed sign cube, the variance
of the function $x\mapsto a_i x_i$ is $a_i^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Third-moment sum for Rademacher summands]
\lean{FABL.thirdMomentSum_rademacherSummand}
\label{FABL.thirdMomentSum_rademacherSummand}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.integral_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.rademacherMeasure, FABL.rademacherSummand, FABL.signValue_eq_neg_one_or_one}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ be real numbers. For
independent uniform signs $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the sum of the third absolute moments of the
summands $a_iX_i$ is $\sum_{i=1}^n |a_i|^3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Third-moment bound for normalized Rademacher sums]
\lean{FABL.thirdMomentSum_rademacherSummand_le}
\label{FABL.thirdMomentSum_rademacherSummand_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.rademacherMeasure, FABL.rademacherSummand, FABL.thirdMomentSum_rademacherSummand}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ be real numbers satisfying
$\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2=1$. If $|a_i|\le\varepsilon$ for every $i$, then for independent
uniform signs $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the sum of the third absolute moments of the summands
$a_iX_i$ is at most $\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\label{FABL.standardGaussian_hasSubgaussianMGF}
\leanok
\difficulty{3}
The identity random variable on the real line, distributed according to the standard
Gaussian measure, has a sub-Gaussian moment-generating function with parameter $1$.
\end{theorem}

\label{FABL.measureReal_abs_ge_le_two_mul_exp}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
Let $(\Omega,\mu)$ be a probability space, let $Y:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ have sub-Gaussian
moment-generating function with parameter $1$, and let $t\ge 0$. Then $\mu(\{\omega:
t\le |Y(\omega)|\})\le 2\exp(-t^2/2)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Sub-Gaussian tails for Rademacher and Gaussian sums]
\lean{FABL.exercise5_31a}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p137-b012}
\label{FABL.exercise5_31a}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.linearForm, FABL.measureReal_abs_ge_le_two_mul_exp, FABL.rademacherLinearForm_hasSubgaussianMGF, FABL.rademacherMeasure, FABL.standardGaussian_hasSubgaussianMGF}
\difficulty{1}
Let $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $\sum_i a_i^2=1$, and suppose
$|a_i|\leq\varepsilon$ for every $i$. For every $t\geq0$, if $X$ is uniform on
$\{-1,1\}^n$ and $Z$ is standard Gaussian, then both $\mathbb{P}(|\sum_i a_iX_i|\geq t)$
and $\mathbb{P}(|Z|\geq t)$ are at most $2e^{-t^2/2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Absolute tail]
\lean{FABL.absoluteTail}
\label{FABL.absoluteTail}
\leanok
For a measure $\nu$ on $\mathbb R$ and a real number $t$, define its absolute tail at
$t$ to be the measure of $\{x\in\mathbb R:t<|x|\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Measurability of the absolute tail]
\lean{FABL.measurable_absoluteTail}
\label{FABL.measurable_absoluteTail}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.absoluteTail}
\difficulty{3}
For every finite measure $\nu$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the function $t\mapsto
\nu(\{x\in\mathbb{R}:t<|x|\})$ is measurable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Integrability of the absolute tail]
\lean{FABL.integrableOn_absoluteTail}
\label{FABL.integrableOn_absoluteTail}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.absoluteTail, FABL.measurable_absoluteTail}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\nu$ be a finite measure on $\mathbb{R}$ such that $x\mapsto |x|$ is integrable
with respect to $\nu$. For $t\in\mathbb{R}$, define the absolute tail as the measure of
$\{x\in\mathbb{R}:t<|x|\}$. This tail is integrable as a function of $t$ on
$(0,\infty)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[First absolute moment bound from tail control]
\lean{FABL.abs_integral_abs_sub_le_of_absoluteTail}
\label{FABL.abs_integral_abs_sub_le_of_absoluteTail}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.absoluteTail, FABL.integrableOn_absoluteTail}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\\nu$ and $\\tau$ be finite measures on $\\mathbb R$ with integrable absolute-value
functions, and let $B:\\mathbb R\\to\\mathbb R$ be integrable on $(0,\\infty)$. If for
every $t>0$ the absolute difference between $\\nu(\\{x:|x|>t\\})$ and
$\\tau(\\{x:|x|>t\\})$ is at most $B(t)$, then the absolute difference between their
first absolute moments is at most $\\int_0^\\infty B(t)\\,dt$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Absolute tail as a complement probability]
\lean{FABL.absoluteTail_eq_one_sub_interval}
\label{FABL.absoluteTail_eq_one_sub_interval}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.absoluteTail}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\nu$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb R$, and let $t\ge 0$. The measure of the
set $\{x\in\mathbb R:t<|x|\}$ is one minus the measure of the interval $[-t,t]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Absolute tail error from interval error]
\lean{FABL.absoluteTail_error_le_of_interval_error}
\label{FABL.absoluteTail_error_le_of_interval_error}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.absoluteTail, FABL.absoluteTail_eq_one_sub_interval}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\nu$ and $\tau$ be probability measures on $\mathbb R$, and let $B,t\in\mathbb R$
with $t\ge 0$. If $|\nu([-t,t])-\tau([-t,t])|\le B$, then the absolute tail
probabilities of $\nu$ and $\tau$ at $t$ differ by at most $B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}[Nonuniform Gaussian CDF error bound]
\lean{FABL.strictCdfError_le_nonuniform}
\label{FABL.strictCdfError_le_nonuniform}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.gaussianReal_cdf_leftLim, FABL.measureReal_Iio_eq_leftLim_cdf}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\nu$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$, and let $K\in\mathbb{R}$. If for
every $y\in\mathbb{R}$ the difference between the distribution functions of $\nu$ and
the standard Gaussian is bounded in absolute value by $K/(1+|y|^3)$, then for every
$x\in\mathbb{R}$, $\left|\nu((-\infty,x))-\Phi(x)\right|\le K/(1+|x|^3)$, where $\Phi$
is the standard Gaussian distribution function.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Absolute tail error from a nonuniform distribution bound]
\lean{FABL.absoluteTail_error_le_nonuniform}
\label{FABL.absoluteTail_error_le_nonuniform}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.absoluteTail, FABL.absoluteTail_error_le_of_interval_error, FABL.strictCdfError_le_nonuniform}
\difficulty{5}
Let $\nu$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb R$, and let $K,t\in\mathbb R$ with $t\ge
0$. If for every $x\in\mathbb R$ the distribution functions of $\nu$ and the standard
Gaussian satisfy $|F_\nu(x)-\Phi(x)|\le K/(1+|x|^3)$, then their absolute tail
probabilities at $t$ differ by at most $2K/(1+t^3)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Comparison of reciprocal polynomial tails]
\lean{FABL.inv_one_add_cube_le_two_mul_inv_one_add_sq}
\label{FABL.inv_one_add_cube_le_two_mul_inv_one_add_sq}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
For every real number $t\ge0$, $$(1+t^3)^{-1}\le 2(1+t^2)^{-1}.$$
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Integrability of a reciprocal cubic function]
\lean{FABL.integrableOn_inv_one_add_cube}
\label{FABL.integrableOn_inv_one_add_cube}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.inv_one_add_cube_le_two_mul_inv_one_add_sq}
\difficulty{4}
The function $t\mapsto (1+t^3)^{-1}$ is integrable on $(0,\infty)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[A bound for a cubic reciprocal integral]
\lean{FABL.integral_Ioi_inv_one_add_cube_le_four}
\label{FABL.integral_Ioi_inv_one_add_cube_le_four}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.integrableOn_inv_one_add_cube, FABL.inv_one_add_cube_le_two_mul_inv_one_add_sq}
\difficulty{4}
The integral of $(1+t^3)^{-1}$ over $t>0$ is at most $4$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Integrability of a cubic tail bound]
\lean{FABL.integrableOn_nonuniformTailBound}
\label{FABL.integrableOn_nonuniformTailBound}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.integrableOn_inv_one_add_cube}
\difficulty{1}
For every real number $K$, the function $t\mapsto 2K/(1+t^3)$ is integrable on
$(0,\infty)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Integral bound for a rational tail]
\lean{FABL.integral_nonuniformTailBound_le}
\label{FABL.integral_nonuniformTailBound_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.integral_Ioi_inv_one_add_cube_le_four}
\difficulty{3}
For every real number $K\ge0$,
\[\int_0^\infty \frac{2K}{1+t^3}\,dt\le 8K.\]
\end{theorem}

\label{FABL.measureReal_Ioi_eq_one_sub_cdf}
\leanok
\difficulty{1}
If $\nu$ is a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$, then for every $t\in\mathbb{R}$,
$\nu((t,\infty))=1-F_\nu(t)$, where $F_\nu(t)=\nu((-\infty,t])$ is its cumulative
distribution function.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Measurability of an upper tail function]
\lean{FABL.measurable_upperTailFrom}
\label{FABL.measurable_upperTailFrom}
\leanok
\difficulty{3}
For every finite measure $\nu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and every $t\in\mathbb{R}$, the function
$u\mapsto \nu((t+u,\infty))$ is measurable on $\mathbb{R}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Positive-part threshold set]
\lean{FABL.setOf_lt_posPart_sub_eq_Ioi_add}
\label{FABL.setOf_lt_posPart_sub_eq_Ioi_add}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
For real numbers $t$ and $u$ with $u>0$, the set of real $z$ satisfying $u<\max(z-t,0)$
is the open interval $(t+u,\infty)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Integrability of an upper-tail function]
\lean{FABL.integrableOn_upperTailFrom}
\label{FABL.integrableOn_upperTailFrom}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.measurable_upperTailFrom, FABL.setOf_lt_posPart_sub_eq_Ioi_add}
\difficulty{5}
Let $\nu$ be a finite measure on $\mathbb{R}$, and let $t\in\mathbb{R}$. Suppose that
$z\mapsto\max(z-t,0)$ is integrable with respect to $\nu$. Then the function
$u\mapsto\nu((t+u,\infty))$ is integrable on $(0,\infty)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Positive-part integral as an upper-tail integral]
\lean{FABL.integral_posPart_sub_eq_integral_upperTailFrom}
\label{FABL.integral_posPart_sub_eq_integral_upperTailFrom}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.setOf_lt_posPart_sub_eq_Ioi_add}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\nu$ be a measure on $\mathbb R$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. If the function
$z\mapsto(z-t)^+$ is integrable with respect to $\nu$, then
\[\int_{\mathbb R}(z-t)^+\,d\nu(z)=\int_0^\infty \nu_{\mathrm{real}}\bigl((t+u,\infty)\bigr)\,du.\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[A Gaussian-weighted tail integral]
\lean{FABL.integral_Ioi_mul_exp_neg_sq_div_two}
\label{FABL.integral_Ioi_mul_exp_neg_sq_div_two}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
The integral of $x\exp(-x^2/2)$ over $x>0$ equals $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Positive part mean of a standard Gaussian]
\lean{FABL.integral_posPart_standardGaussian}
\label{FABL.integral_posPart_standardGaussian}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.integral_Ioi_mul_exp_neg_sq_div_two}
\difficulty{5}
If $X$ has the standard Gaussian distribution on $\mathbb R$, then
\[\mathbb E[X^+]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}},\]
where $X^+=\max(X,0)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Gaussian normalization identity]
\lean{FABL.two_mul_inv_sqrt_two_mul_pi}
\label{FABL.two_mul_inv_sqrt_two_mul_pi}
\leanok
\difficulty{3}
The identity $2(\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}=\sqrt{2/\pi}$ holds.
\end{theorem}

  {pdf-681b6f3d947f-p015-b002,
    pdf-681b6f3d947f-p015-b003}
\difficulty{3}
Let $\nu$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ whose moment-generating function
satisfies the subgaussian bound with parameter $1$. For every $t\ge 0$, the measure of
$\{x\in\mathbb{R}:t<|x|\}$ is at most $2e^{-t^2/2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Truncated tail bound]
\lean{FABL.truncatedTailBound}
\statementsource{vershynin-hdp-book}{pdf-681b6f3d947f-p023-b001}
\label{FABL.truncatedTailBound}
\leanok
For real numbers $U,T,t$, define the truncated tail bound to equal $U$ when $t\le T$,
and to equal $4\exp(-t^2/2)$ when $t>T$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Integrability of a truncated tail bound]
\lean{FABL.integrableOn_truncatedTailBound}
\label{FABL.integrableOn_truncatedTailBound}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.truncatedTailBound}
\difficulty{5}
For real numbers $U$ and $T$ with $T\ge 0$, define a function of $t\in\mathbb{R}$ to
equal $U$ when $t\le T$, and $4\exp(-t^2/2)$ when $t>T$. This function is integrable on
$(0,\infty)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Integral bound for a truncated tail]
\lean{FABL.integral_truncatedTailBound_le}
\label{FABL.integral_truncatedTailBound_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.integrableOn_truncatedTailBound, FABL.truncatedTailBound}
\difficulty{6}
Let $U,T\in\mathbb{R}$ with $1\le T$, and define $g(t)=U$ for $t\le T$ and
$g(t)=4\exp(-t^2/2)$ for $t>T$. Then the integral of $g$ over $t>0$ is at most
$UT+4\exp(-T^2/2)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform linear approximation for the absolute Rademacher sum]
\lean{FABL.exercise5_31d}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p137-b012}
\label{FABL.exercise5_31d}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.abs_integral_abs_sub_le_of_absoluteTail, FABL.absoluteTail_error_le_nonuniform, FABL.integrableOn_nonuniformTailBound, FABL.integral_abs_standardGaussian, FABL.integral_nonuniformTailBound_le, FABL.integral_rademacherSummand_eq_zero, FABL.integral_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.linearForm, FABL.rademacherLinearForm_hasSubgaussianMGF, FABL.rademacherMeasure, FABL.rademacherSummand, FABL.rademacherSummand_memLp, FABL.rademacherSummands_iIndep, FABL.sum_rademacherSummand, FABL.thirdMomentSum_rademacherSummand_le, FABL.variance_rademacherSummand}
\difficulty{5}
There exists a constant $C>0$ such that, for every natural number $n$, every
$a_1,\dots,a_n\in\mathbb R$ with $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2=1$, and every
$\varepsilon\in\mathbb R$ satisfying $|a_i|\le\varepsilon$ for all $i$, independent
uniform signs $X_1,\dots,X_n\in\{-1,1\}$ satisfy
\[
\left|\mathbb E\left|\sum_{i=1}^n a_iX_i\right|-\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\right|\le
C\varepsilon.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Stop-loss approximation for Rademacher sums]
\lean{FABL.exists_stopLoss_linearForm_sub_standardGaussian_le_of_regular}
\label{FABL.exists_stopLoss_linearForm_sub_standardGaussian_le_of_regular}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.integrableOn_nonuniformTailBound, FABL.integrableOn_upperTailFrom, FABL.integral_nonuniformTailBound_le, FABL.integral_posPart_sub_eq_integral_upperTailFrom, FABL.integral_rademacherSummand_eq_zero, FABL.integral_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.linearForm, FABL.measureReal_Ioi_eq_one_sub_cdf, FABL.rademacherLinearForm_hasSubgaussianMGF, FABL.rademacherMeasure, FABL.rademacherSummand, FABL.rademacherSummand_memLp, FABL.rademacherSummands_iIndep, FABL.sum_rademacherSummand, FABL.thirdMomentSum_rademacherSummand_le, FABL.variance_rademacherSummand}
\difficulty{6}
There is a constant $C>0$ such that, for every $n$, every coefficient vector
$a\in\mathbb R^n$ with $\sum_i a_i^2=1$, every $\varepsilon>0$ satisfying
$|a_i|\le\varepsilon$ for all $i$, and every $t\ge0$, the stop-loss expectation of the
Rademacher sum $\sum_i a_i x_i$ differs from that of a standard Gaussian by at most
$C\varepsilon$:
\[\left|\mathbb E_x\left(\sum_i a_i x_i-t\right)^+-\int_{\mathbb R}(z-t)^+\,d\gamma(z)\right|\le C\varepsilon,\]
where $x$ is uniform on the sign cube and $\gamma$ is the standard Gaussian measure.
\end{theorem}

    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p128-b002}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\sum_{i=1}^n
a_i^2=1$ and $|a_i|\le\varepsilon$ for every $i$. If $T\ge1$, then for independent
uniform signs $X_1,\dots,X_n\in\{-1,1\}$,
\[
\left|\mathbb E\left|\sum_{i=1}^n a_iX_i\right|-\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\right|\le
2K\varepsilon T+4e^{-T^2/2},
\]
where $K$ is the third-moment Berry–Esseen constant.
\end{theorem}

  {FABL.exercise5_31b}
  {direct}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p119-b005,
    pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p137-b011}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $a_1,\dots,a_n\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\sum_{i=1}^n
a_i^2=1$ and $|a_i|\le\varepsilon$ for every $i$, where $0<\varepsilon\le e^{-1}$. For
independent uniform signs $X_1,\dots,X_n\in\{-1,1\}$,
\[
\left|\mathbb E\left|\sum_{i=1}^n a_iX_i\right|-\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\right|\le
4(K+1)\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)},
\]
where $K$ is the third-moment Berry–Esseen constant.
\end{theorem}

  {FABL.exercise5_31d}
  {direct}
  {Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}
  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p119-b005}
\difficulty{1}
There is a constant $C>0$ such that for every dimension $n$, every coefficient vector
$a\in\mathbb R^n$ with $\sum_i a_i^2=1$, and every real $\varepsilon$ satisfying
$|a_i|\le\varepsilon$ for all $i$, the expected absolute value of the corresponding
linear form on a uniformly random Boolean-cube point differs from $\sqrt{2/\pi}$ by at
most $C\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}
